title: I ran 5 algorithmic trading bots as one portfolio for 6 months: +298%, −12.7% max drawdown (simulation, fees included)
author: alucard666_0
selftext:
I trade with a small set of automated bots, and I wanted to evaluate them the way you'd evaluate a fund: not "which bot is best", but what the **combined** curve looks like, with drawdowns in plain sight. Most posts about trading bots show one green screenshot, so I'm sharing the full picture, including the parts that don't flatter it.

**What this is**

* 5 bots, each trading its own signal, run together as one portfolio from May 20 to Nov 20, 2026 (185 days), on 12 crypto assets.
* A **simulation** on the bots' signal history, not a live account statement. The same bots have also been run in real-money tests, but the numbers below are the simulation.
* **Fees: 0.12% deducted from every round trip** (entry + exit), already inside every number. That's deliberately above typical exchange fees, to leave room for slippage and holding costs like funding.
* Open positions are marked to market. **More than a third of the total (+105.5 of +298.2) is still open**, not closed.

**How the % are computed (read this before the numbers)**

* Everything is **% of starting capital**. Each bot's trades are sized by a fixed weight, so every trade's PnL is converted to its effect on the account.
* **Not compounded**: position size doesn't grow with profits.
* The bots overlap, so at times total exposure is above 1× the capital.
* Absolute drops (per-bot max DD, monthly changes) are in **percentage points (pp) of starting capital**, so they don't read like a % of the account. Drawdown from the peak is in % of the account.
* Win rate is per trade. Avg/best/worst trade are each trade's effect on the account, after the weight.

**Headline numbers**

* Combined: **+298.2%** (realized +192.7%, still open +105.5%)
* Max drawdown: **−12.7% from peak equity** (Sep 23 → Nov 5). The curve went from +264% to +217%, a 46 pp drop. This is mark-to-market: the peak includes profit on positions that were still open, and giving that back counts.
* Measured on closed trades only, the worst drop is **−8.1%** (Oct 29 → Nov 6). I'm leading with the 12.7% on purpose: it's the harsher way to measure it.
* 826 closed trades, **32.1% win rate**
* Longest stretch without a new high: **57 days**; the curve spent **85.9% of days below a previous high**
* Months, in pp of starting capital: May +5.6, Jun +93.2, Jul −3.7, Aug +105.7, Sep +54.5, **Oct −24.0** (≈ −6.7% of the account at the time), Nov +66.8 so far

**Per bot**

Return in % of starting capital, Max DD in percentage points of it.

|Bot|Return|Share|Trades|Win rate|Avg/trade|Max DD (pp)|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Horus 2|\+105.2%|35.3%|168|50.6%|\+0.65%|−14.4|
|White Line|\+79.1%|26.5%|43|32.6%|\+0.34%|−23.2|
|Horus|\+55.3%|18.5%|315|19.0%|\+0.18%|−14.9|
|Sentiment × Horus|\+49.6%|16.6%|113|41.6%|\+0.45%|−13.3|
|Grid Basic|\+9.0%|3.0%|187|31.6%|−0.03%|−13.3|

**What I take from it (and what worries me)**

* **Low win rate, positive expectancy.** Horus wins 19% of the time and is still positive, because losers are small (worst trade −0.28%) and a few winners are big. That only works if you never skip the boring losing streaks.
* **Concentration.** Horus 2 is the top contributor, but White Line gets 26.5% of the result from only 43 trades, and its single best trade (+26.5%) is about a third of its total. It also has the deepest drawdown of the five (23 pp).
* **Grid Basic is a drag in this window.** Its average trade is −0.03% over 187 trades after fees, and its +9.0% comes from the curve, not from the average trade. It does move independently (0.12 daily correlation with the other four), but independence didn't help: without Grid the biggest drop would have been 42.1 pp instead of 46.4, and return / max drawdown 6.87 instead of 6.43. On the 23 days when the others lost more than 5 pp, Grid averaged −0.6 pp. I'm keeping it for now only because a window this short is a small sample.
* **Diversification helps, but it's not magic.** The five individual biggest drops add up to 79 pp of starting capital, while the combined curve's worst drop was 46 pp, so they didn't all bottom out together. It still fell 12.7% from peak equity in Sep–Nov.
* **A third of the result isn't banked yet.** Realized is +192.7%, the rest is open positions marked to market. If those close worse, the total falls with them.

**Benchmark, done carefully**

Equal-weight buy & hold on 12 coins did −20.1% with a 37.8% max drawdown over the same window, at 1× exposure. The two don't run the same risk, so I didn't overlay them raw: I scaled buy & hold by 0.95 so its **biggest drop is the same** as the bots' (46 pp of starting capital). At equal pain: bots +272%, buy & hold −19%. It's the fairest comparison I could think of; happy to hear better ones.

**Questions for you**

1. How do you combine several strategies: equal weight, inverse volatility, inverse drawdown, something learned?
2. Would you cut a strategy like Grid Basic that is uncorrelated but slightly negative per trade?
3. How would you stress-test the White Line concentration problem?
4. What would convince you that a simulation like this is out-of-sample enough to trust?

Not financial advice. Trading involves risk of losing capital, and past (simulated) results don't predict future ones.

The same data as a 38-second clip: (1) the combined curve drawing itself, with the Sep 23 → Nov 5 drawdown in red; (2) bots vs buy & hold scaled to the same biggest drop, with both drawdown curves underneath; (3) each bot's own curve, one by one, on the same scale.

replies.author: CryptoLamboMoon
replies.body: Paper strategies without live tests are just paper

replies.author: alucard666_0
replies.body: Fair point, and I agree: a simulation isn’t a track record, which is why I labeled it as one. The same bots have also been run with real money, but I’m not presenting those results here, only the simulation, so nobody has to take the live side on trust.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the +105.5 that's still open is the number I'd watch. marked to market on crypto, a third of the curve can vanish in one bad weekend, so a closed-trades-only version of the same table would say a lot more.

replies.author: alucard666_0
replies.body:
Agreed, it's the number I'd watch too. Closed trades only, same window and fees (closed / open / total, in % of starting capital, not compounded):



Horus 2: +87.4 / +17.9 / +105.2

Sentiment x Horus: +49.6 / 0 / +49.6

Horus: +38.9 / +16.4 / +55.3

White Line: +21.6 / +57.4 / +79.1

Grid Basic: -4.8 / +13.8 / +9.0

TOTAL: +192.7 / +105.5 / +298.2



Closed-only max drawdown is 23.9 pp, about 8.1% of the account (Oct 29 to Nov 6).



The most useful part: White Line is mostly open (+57 of its +79), so on closed trades it drops from 2nd to 4th, and Grid goes slightly negative. Horus 2 and Sentiment x Horus carry the closed result.



On the weekend risk: the worst 3-day move of the total curve in this sample was -18.8 pp, but the curve is coarsely sampled and 6 months isn't a stress test, so I wouldn't read that as safe.

comments.author: tru3relativity
comments.body: Can you tell us anything about these strategies?

replies.author: alucard666_0
replies.body:
Only at a high level, since the edge is in the details. The five bots are a mix of types: two are momentum-driven and score-based (one is a variant of the other), one is a breakout-style entry with a second layer of confirmation, one trades rarely on high-conviction setups, and one is a plain grid bot.

The win rates differ a lot between them (from about 19% to about 50%). Some win rarely with small losers and a few big winners, others win about half the time. The grid bot is mostly there as a diversifier, and it’s the one I’m least sure about keeping.

comments.author: cybersarcasm
comments.body:
Appreciate you leading with the 12.7% drawdown instead of the green screenshot. A few questions:



1. Were the signals logged live as they fired between May 20 and Nov 20, or regenerated afterward from the bots' current code? Were any parameters tuned using data from this window?

2. How were these 5 chosen? How many bots did you run or test in total before landing on this set?

3. You mention real-money tests. Over the same stretch, how did live fills compare with the simulation, in return and in number of trades actually filled?

4. White Line: what's its return with its best 3 trades removed?

replies.author: alucard666_0
replies.body:
Thanks for the questions, they’re the right ones.

**1. Live vs regenerated.** The raw signals are recorded as they fire. Some bots use a static journal of those signals. Others are recalculated afterwards, for example to apply the sizing rules. So this isn’t a pure live record, and it isn’t a pure regeneration either. I can’t claim no parameter was ever tuned on data that overlaps this window.

**2. Selection.** The 5 were picked from about two years of tests, using backtest samples going back up to 8 years. That means this 6 month window falls inside the period used for selection, so please don’t read it as clean out of sample. It’s a portfolio view of strategies I already trusted, not a blind test.

**3. Live vs simulation.** The simulation charges 0.12% per round trip. Real fees are lower than that, and funding has often been positive for me, so live costs have come out better than the simulation assumes. I’m not quoting a live return figure here because it isn’t a like for like comparison with the simulation.

**4. White Line.** It’s built to trade rarely and capture big moves, and that’s how it behaves in my longer backtests too: few trades, high returns per trade, but slow. That also makes it lumpy in a 6 month window. On closed trades only it’s +21.6 pp, and its single best trade is +26.5 pp, so without that one it’s about −5. Without the best three, roughly −12. The rest of its +79 is still open. With only 43 trades here, this window is too short to judge it, and I’d rather say that than defend the number.

comments.body: Bro that's like 5 trades, plus a lot of sideways. What.

comments.author: AmWoz
comments.body: That is a lot to read so I thought I'd ask the question is this purely paper trades? Because something I noticed on paper is it always can fill and has no latency making the results better have you found a way to properly compare that kind of stuff?

replies.author: alucard666_0
replies.body: Yes, the numbers in the post are a simulation, so it assumes fills at the signal price with no latency. That’s the main way a sim flatters results. To compensate, I charge 0.12% per round trip, which is above real exchange fees, to leave room for slippage and funding. I’ve also run the same bots with real money, and on costs live has come out better than the sim assumes (lower fees, often positive funding).

comments.author: thedaywalker11
comments.body: What method are you using? Price action?

replies.author: alucard666_0
replies.body: Not pure price action. It’s a mix: momentum and score-based signals, breakout-style entries, a grid bot, and one that waits for several indicators to line up. They’re different families on purpose, so they don’t all fail at the same time.
